title: Scroll-to-Top on Every Navigation
summary: This commands ensures that when a user lands on any page of an application, the user gets taken to the very top of that page, and not the position the user was on the previous page.
tags: top of the page;page position;fixed page position
body:
Make every navigation in my app start at the top of the new page.

Stack: {{stack}}
Exceptions that must keep or restore scroll position: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. On each route change, scroll to (0, 0) before or as the new page paints, so there's no visible jump.
2. Respect the exceptions above. Browser back/forward should restore the previous position unless I said otherwise, and links to #anchors should scroll to the anchor.
3. Handle scrollable containers too, not just window, if the layout scrolls inside a main element.
4. Move keyboard focus to the new page's main heading so screen-reader users know the page changed.
5. Use the framework's built-in mechanism if it has one before writing custom code, and explain why.

Tell me how to test it: three navigation scenarios to click through and what should happen in each.

title: Universal Dark-Mode Toggle
summary: Persist a user’s light/dark preference across sessions and devices.
body:
Add a light/dark theme toggle that remembers each person's choice.

Stack: {{stack}}
Default for new visitors: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Three options: Light, Dark and System. Apply the default above until someone chooses.
2. Save the choice in localStorage, and in the user's profile when they're logged in, so it follows them across devices.
3. Apply the theme before first paint (an inline script or server-rendered class), so there's no flash of the wrong theme.
4. Drive colors from CSS variables, and check text contrast meets WCAG AA in both themes.
5. The toggle must be a real button with an accessible name and the current state announced.

List the files you'll change, then give me a test checklist: first visit, switch and reload, log in on a second browser, and system theme changes.

title: Instant Email Verification Link
summary: Verify new accounts seamlessly
body:
Add email verification to sign-up.

Stack: {{stack}}
Until they verify, users may: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. On sign-up, send a single-use, signed verification link that expires after 24 hours. Store only a hash of the token.
2. Enforce the restriction above on the server, not just in the UI.
3. Let people resend the link (rate-limited) and show a clear message when a link is expired or already used.
4. Clicking the link marks email_verified = true and logs them in or sends them to log in, depending on how our auth works.
5. Don't reveal whether an email address has an account on the resend form.

Tell me which files change, what the email says, and how to test the whole flow locally, including an expired link.

title: One-Click Password Reset
summary: Fast, secure password recovery
body:
Add a secure "Forgot password" flow.

Stack: {{stack}}
After a successful reset, send people to: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. The request form always shows the same message, whether or not the email has an account.
2. Send a single-use token that expires in 60 minutes; store only its hash. Rate-limit requests per email and IP.
3. The reset page checks the token, enforces our password rules, and then invalidates the token and every other active session.
4. Email the user that their password was changed, with a way to report it wasn't them.
5. Redirect as described above, with a confirmation message.

List the files you'll change and give me a test plan, including reusing a token, an expired token and two tabs requesting resets.

title: Autosave Form Drafts
summary: Prevent data loss on long forms
body:
Autosave drafts so people never lose a long form.

Stack: {{stack}}
Form: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Save changed fields locally (IndexedDB, keyed by form and user) a few seconds after typing stops, not on every keystroke.
2. When the person comes back before submitting, offer to restore the draft and show when it was saved.
3. Clear the draft after a successful submit or when they choose "Discard".
4. Never store passwords, card numbers or other sensitive fields; list which fields you excluded.
5. Show a quiet "Saved" indicator, and handle two tabs editing the same form without overwriting each other silently.

List the files you'll change, then give me a test plan: type, reload, close the tab, come back, submit, and the two-tab case.

title: Debounced Live Search
summary: Reduce server load while users type
body:
Add live search that updates as people type without overloading the server.

Stack: {{stack}}
Search covers: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Debounce input by about 300 ms and send one request with the final query.
2. Cancel in-flight requests when a newer query starts, so older results never overwrite newer ones.
3. Skip requests for queries shorter than 2 characters; trim whitespace.
4. Show loading, empty ("No results for …") and error states, and keep the previous results visible while the next ones load.
5. Make results keyboard-navigable (arrow keys, Enter, Escape) and announce the result count to screen readers.
6. Reflect the query in the URL so searches can be shared and the back button works.

Explain how to verify it: what the network tab should show while typing quickly, and the edge cases you tested.

title: Skeleton Loading Placeholders
summary: Smooth perceived performance
body:
Replace blank or spinner states with skeleton placeholders.

Stack: {{stack}}
Start with these screens: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Skeletons match the final layout (same size and position), so nothing shifts when data arrives. Aim for zero layout shift.
2. Show them only while data is actually loading; if loading takes under ~150 ms, don't flash them.
3. Use the framework's loading/streaming features where they exist instead of hand-rolled state.
4. Add a subtle shimmer that is disabled when the user prefers reduced motion.
5. Mark loading regions with aria-busy and keep the skeletons hidden from screen readers.

Show me one reusable skeleton component, then apply it to the screens above. Tell me how to see it locally (for example by throttling the network in DevTools).

title: Graceful 404 Fallback
summary: Keep users oriented on bad URLs
body:
Add a graceful 404 experience to my app.

Stack: {{stack}}
Lost visitors should be steered to: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Catch every unmatched route (including nested and dynamic segments) and render a branded 404 page that returns a real HTTP 404 status, not a 200.
2. Show a short, human message, a primary button that takes people to {{goal}}, and a search box that searches the site.
3. Log the missing path to our error analytics, but strip query strings, emails, tokens and IDs before sending.
4. Keep the normal header and navigation so the page doesn't feel like a dead end.
5. Make it accessible: one h1, focus moves to the heading on load, the button and search work with the keyboard.

Before changing code, list the files you'll touch. After, give me:
- the exact steps to test it (a URL that should 404, what I should see, and how to confirm the status code in DevTools or with curl -I)
- anything you couldn't verify.

title: Role-Based Access Control
summary: Limit sensitive features to the right people
body:
Add role-based access control.

Stack: {{stack}}
Roles and permissions: {{goal}}

Requirements:
1. Define the roles and permissions above in one place in code, and check permissions (not role names) at each use.
2. Enforce access on the server for every protected page, API route and mutation. Hiding buttons in the UI is not enough.
3. Deny by default: new routes are blocked until they declare the permission they need.
4. Return 403 (not 404 or 500) for authenticated users without permission, and log the denial.
5. Keep roles somewhere the client can't edit (server-side session or database), and make role changes take effect on the next request.

List the files you'll change, then give me a test matrix: each role against each protected action, with the expected result.

title: Local Business Directory System
summary: A full template including initial command and knowledge base to build a local business directory service that you can apply to your local community and start helping small businesses while making a profit.
body:
Plan and build a local business directory for: {{goal}}

Stack: {{stack}}

Build it in this order, and stop after each phase so I can review:

Phase 1: Directory
1. Searchable listings with name, description, contact details, address, opening hours and photos.
2. Keyword search plus filters for category and neighborhood.
3. A "Contact this business" form that sends inquiries to the business and records them as leads.

Phase 2: Accounts and reviews
4. Visitor accounts to save favorites and leave reviews (one per business per person, with moderation).
5. Business owners can claim and edit their listing after verification.

Phase 3: Admin and revenue
6. An admin panel to approve, edit and remove listings, moderate reviews and see leads.
7. Paid placements (featured listings, banners) with clear "Sponsored" labels.
8. A simple analytics dashboard: views, leads and revenue per listing.

Throughout: comply with privacy law for the area above, secure the admin panel, keep pages fast on mobile, and write clear error messages.

Start with Phase 1: propose the data model and pages, list the files you'll create, and wait for my go-ahead.

title: Build an accessible React component
summary: Get a production-ready component with keyboard support, ARIA and tests.
body:
Build a {{component}} component in React + TypeScript for {{use_case}}.

Requirements:
- Fully keyboard operable (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrow keys where it makes sense).
- Correct roles and ARIA attributes; no ARIA where native HTML already works.
- Visible focus styles that pass WCAG 2.2 AA contrast.
- Props are typed, documented with JSDoc, and have sensible defaults.
- No external UI libraries. Styling with {{styling}}.

Return: the component file, a short usage example, and a test file (Testing Library) covering keyboard use and screen-reader labels.

title: Pre-launch UI polish checklist
summary: Walk a page through the details users notice before you ship.
body:
Review the page at {{page_url_or_file}} against this checklist and report each item as PASS / FIX with a one-line note:

1. Empty, loading and error states exist for every data-driven area.
2. Text never overflows or truncates without a tooltip at 320px width.
3. Tap targets are at least 44x44px on mobile.
4. Buttons show a pressed / disabled / busy state.
5. Forms keep user input after a failed submit.
6. Images have width/height (no layout shift) and meaningful alt text.
7. Dark mode (if supported) has no unreadable text.
8. Page title and meta description are set.
9. Keyboard focus order follows visual order.
10. Nothing logs errors to the console.

End with the three fixes that would most improve the page.

title: Convert a design screenshot into clean HTML/CSS
summary: Turn a mockup into semantic, responsive markup without a framework.
body:
I'm attaching a screenshot of {{screen_name}}. Recreate it as semantic HTML and modern CSS.

Rules:
- Mobile first; breakpoints at {{breakpoints}}.
- Use CSS custom properties for colors, spacing and radius; put them in :root.
- Flexbox/grid only, no absolute positioning for layout.
- Use real elements (nav, main, section, button, label) — no div soup.
- Where the screenshot is ambiguous, pick the simplest option and list your assumptions at the end.

Output one HTML file with a <style> block.

title: Find and fix React re-render problems
summary: Diagnose why a component tree is slow and get concrete fixes.
body:
Here is a React component tree that feels slow when {{slow_interaction}}:

{{code}}

1. List every component that re-renders on that interaction and why (props identity, context, state placement).
2. Rank the causes by likely cost.
3. Propose the smallest fixes first (moving state down, splitting context, stable callbacks, memo) and show the changed code.
4. Tell me how to confirm the fix with React DevTools Profiler.

Do not add memoization everywhere — only where it measurably helps.

title: Form validation schema with friendly errors
summary: Generate a Zod schema plus human error messages for any form.
body:
Create a Zod schema for a {{form_name}} form with these fields:
{{fields}}

For each field:
- Pick the right type and constraints (min/max, email, url, regex).
- Write an error message a non-technical person understands ("Use at least 8 characters", not "String must contain at least 8 character(s)").
- Trim strings and coerce numbers where appropriate.

Also export the inferred TypeScript type and a helper that turns Zod errors into { field: message } for the UI.

title: Design a REST API for a feature
summary: Endpoints, payloads, status codes and edge cases before you write code.
body:
Design a REST API for {{feature}} in a {{stack}} app.

Give me:
1. Resources and endpoints (method, path, purpose).
2. Request and response JSON for each, with realistic example values.
3. Status codes for success and every failure case.
4. Auth and permission rules per endpoint.
5. Pagination, filtering and sorting conventions.
6. Idempotency and rate-limit notes for write endpoints.
7. Open questions I need to answer before building.

Keep it consistent: plural nouns, kebab-case paths, camelCase JSON.

title: Model a Postgres schema with row-level security
summary: Tables, indexes and RLS policies for a multi-user feature.
body:
I'm building {{feature}} on Postgres (Supabase). Users: {{user_roles}}.

Produce a single SQL migration that:
- Creates tables with uuid primary keys, timestamps, foreign keys and check constraints.
- Adds indexes for every foreign key and every column I'll filter or sort by.
- Enables RLS on every table and writes select/insert/update/delete policies per role, using (select auth.uid()).
- Keeps privileged logic in security definer functions with search_path set to ''.

After the SQL, explain each policy in one sentence and list queries I should run to prove a user cannot read another user's rows.

title: Add a background job safely
summary: Move slow work out of the request with retries and idempotency.
body:
The request handler below does slow work ({{slow_work}}) inline:

{{code}}

Refactor it to a background job using {{queue_tool}}:
1. The handler validates input, enqueues a job with an idempotency key, and returns 202 immediately.
2. The worker is safe to run twice for the same key.
3. Retries use exponential backoff with a max attempt count; failures land in a dead-letter list.
4. Log job id, attempt and duration; never log secrets or full payloads.
5. Show how the UI can poll or subscribe for the result.

Return the new handler, the worker and a short runbook for stuck jobs.

title: Write integration tests for an endpoint
summary: Cover the happy path, auth and the edge cases that bite in production.
body:
Write integration tests for this endpoint using {{test_framework}}:

{{endpoint_code}}

Cover at minimum:
- Success with valid input (assert body and status).
- Missing/invalid auth → 401/403.
- Validation failures for each required field.
- Not found and conflict cases.
- Rate limit or duplicate submission behavior if present.

Use factories for test data, clean up after each test, and don't mock the database unless I say so.

title: Database migration safety review
summary: Catch locking, data loss and rollback problems before running a migration.
body:
Review this migration before it runs on a production database with {{table_size}} rows:

{{migration_sql}}

Check and report:
1. Statements that take long or exclusive locks (adding NOT NULL, changing types, non-concurrent indexes).
2. Anything that drops or rewrites data — and whether it's reversible.
3. Whether app code that is deployed today keeps working during and after the migration.
4. A safer multi-step version if needed (expand → backfill → contract).
5. The exact rollback steps.

Finish with GO / NO-GO and why.

title: Project context pack for coding agents
summary: A reusable AGENTS.md that stops your AI agent from guessing.
body:
Write an AGENTS.md for my project so coding agents work the way my team does.

Project: {{project_description}}
Stack: {{stack}}

Include sections:
- What this app is and who uses it (3 lines).
- How to run, test, lint and build (exact commands).
- Folder map: where things live and where new code goes.
- Conventions: naming, error handling, data fetching, styling.
- Never do: list of dangerous or banned actions (e.g. editing generated files, touching prod data).
- Definition of done for a change.

Rules for writing it:
- If an AGENTS.md already exists, update it and keep the parts that are still true.
- Only state facts you checked in this repo: run the commands, open the folders. Mark folders that don't exist yet as (planned), and write "no test runner yet" if there isn't one.
- Don't copy your own personal or global instructions into this project file.

Keep it under 120 lines. Prefer concrete rules over advice.

title: Plan → implement → verify loop
summary: Make an AI agent plan first, work in small steps and prove each one.
body:
Task: {{task}}

Work in this loop and do not skip steps:
1. PLAN — Read the relevant files first. Write a numbered plan (max 7 steps), each small enough to verify. List files you'll touch. Stop and wait for "go".
2. IMPLEMENT — Do one step at a time. Match the surrounding code style.
3. VERIFY — After each step run {{verify_command}} and show the result. If it fails, fix before moving on.
4. REPORT — Summarize what changed, what you verified, and anything you skipped or are unsure about.

If you discover the plan is wrong, say so and propose a new plan instead of improvising.

title: Turn a vague request into a precise prompt
summary: Rewrite any rough ask into a prompt with role, context, constraints and output format.
body:
Rewrite my rough request into a strong prompt for an AI model.

My rough request: {{rough_request}}

The rewritten prompt must include:
- Context: who it's for and why.
- The exact task, broken into steps if needed.
- Constraints (length, tone, things to avoid).
- Output format (headings, table, JSON schema...).
- One short example of a good answer if it helps.

Then list up to 3 questions whose answers would make the prompt better. Output the prompt in a code block.

title: Code review as a senior engineer
summary: A focused review that finds real bugs instead of nitpicks.
body:
Review this diff as a senior engineer on a {{stack}} codebase:

{{diff}}

Report only things worth changing, grouped as:
- Bugs (wrong behavior, crashes, races, security) — include a failing scenario for each.
- Risky (missing tests, unclear error handling, performance traps).
- Simplifications that remove code.

Skip formatting and naming nitpicks unless they hide a bug. For each item give file:line, the problem in one sentence, and the fix. End with "ship / ship after fixes / don't ship".

title: Write a reusable AI skill file
summary: Package a repeatable task into instructions an agent can load on demand.
body:
Create a SKILL.md for this repeatable task: {{task_description}}

Format:
---
name: {{skill_name}}
description: One sentence saying exactly when to use this skill.
---

Then:
1. Inputs the agent needs and where to find them.
2. Step-by-step procedure with exact commands or tool calls.
3. Checks that prove the task is done correctly.
4. Common mistakes and how to avoid them.
5. Example of a finished result.

Keep instructions imperative and specific. No filler.

title: GitHub Actions CI for a Node app
summary: Lint, typecheck, test and build on every pull request, with caching.
body:
Write a GitHub Actions workflow for a {{framework}} app using {{package_manager}}.

Requirements:
- Runs on pull_request and push to main.
- Node {{node_version}}, dependency caching keyed on the lockfile.
- Jobs: lint, typecheck, test, build (fail fast; build only after the others pass).
- Cancels in-progress runs for the same branch.
- Uses least-privilege permissions (contents: read).
- No secrets in logs.

Return the YAML and a one-paragraph explanation of each job.

title: Write a minimal production Dockerfile
summary: Small, cached, non-root images for any app.
body:
Write a production Dockerfile for a {{language}} app whose start command is {{start_command}}.

Requirements:
- Multi-stage build; final image based on a slim or distroless base.
- Dependency install layer cached separately from source.
- Runs as a non-root user.
- Only production dependencies in the final image.
- HEALTHCHECK if the app exposes HTTP on {{port}}.
- A matching .dockerignore.

Explain the expected final image size and how to verify it.

title: Incident response first 30 minutes
summary: A calm, ordered playbook for when production is down.
body:
We have an incident: {{symptom}} started at {{start_time}}.

Guide me through the first 30 minutes:
1. Triage: questions to establish scope (who's affected, since when, what changed).
2. Stabilize: safest mitigations in order (roll back last deploy, disable feature flag, scale up, fail over).
3. Communicate: a status-page update and an internal update I can paste now.
4. Investigate: which dashboards, logs and recent changes to check, in order.
5. Record: what to write down for the postmortem while it's fresh.

Ask me for the information you need step by step instead of guessing.

title: Blameless postmortem write-up
summary: Turn incident notes into a postmortem the team will actually read.
body:
Write a blameless postmortem from these notes:

{{incident_notes}}

Sections:
- Summary (3 sentences: what broke, impact, duration).
- Timeline (UTC, key events only).
- Root cause and contributing factors (systems and processes, not people).
- What went well / what was hard.
- Action items: owner, due date, and whether each prevents, detects, or mitigates.

Plain language. No blame, no hedging.

title: Set up structured logging and alerts
summary: Logs you can search and alerts that only fire when it matters.
body:
Set up structured logging and alerting for a {{stack}} service.

1. A logger setup that outputs JSON with timestamp, level, request id, user id (hashed) and duration.
2. Rules for what to log at each level, and what never to log (tokens, passwords, full card numbers, raw PII).
3. Middleware that attaches a request id and logs one line per request.
4. Five alerts worth having for this service, each with a threshold, window and why it matters.
5. How to avoid alert fatigue: grouping, severity and who gets paged.

Show code for the logger and middleware.

title: Threat model a new feature
summary: STRIDE-style review that ends with concrete mitigations.

title: Web app security review
summary: Check an app against the issues attackers try first.
body:
Review {{app_or_code}} against this list. For each, answer PASS / FAIL / N/A with evidence:

1. Every API route checks authentication AND authorization (not just "logged in").
2. User input is validated server-side with an allowlist schema.
3. Queries are parameterized; no string-built SQL.
4. Output is escaped; no dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user data.
5. Secrets are server-only and never shipped to the browser bundle.
6. Cookies are HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite.
7. Rate limits on login, signup, password reset and write endpoints.
8. File uploads check type, size and are re-encoded or scanned.
9. Error messages don't leak stack traces or internal ids.
10. Dependencies have no known critical vulnerabilities.

Finish with the top 3 risks ranked by impact.

title: Find leaked secrets and rotate them
summary: Locate exposed keys in a repo and plan a safe rotation.
body:
I think a secret may have leaked in {{repo_or_location}}.

Help me:
1. Search strategy: commands to scan the working tree and full git history for keys, tokens and passwords (e.g. gitleaks, trufflehog, git log -p with patterns).
2. Triage: how to tell real secrets from test values.
3. Rotation plan for each provider involved ({{providers}}): create new key, deploy it, revoke old key — in an order that avoids downtime.
4. Clean-up: whether rewriting git history is worth it (it doesn't un-leak a pushed secret).
5. Prevention: pre-commit hook and CI scan config.

Never print a full secret value in your answer.

title: Plain-English privacy policy draft
summary: A readable first draft to review with a lawyer.

title: Harden authentication flows
summary: Review sign-up, login and reset flows for common account takeover holes.
body:
Review the authentication flows in {{app_or_code}} (sign-up, login, password reset, email change, session handling).

Check for:
- User enumeration via different error messages or timings.
- Missing rate limits / lockouts.
- Reset tokens that are guessable, long-lived or reusable.
- Email change without re-authentication or confirmation to the old address.
- Sessions not revoked after password change.
- Missing MFA option for admins.

For each issue: the risk, a realistic attack, and the fix with code.

title: Write a SQL query from a plain question
summary: Describe your tables and ask in English; get correct, readable SQL.

title: Explore a new dataset
summary: A first-hour analysis plan for any CSV or table.
body:
I have a dataset: {{dataset_description}} ({{rows}} rows). My goal: {{goal}}.

Walk me through a first-pass exploration in Python (pandas):
1. Load and show shape, dtypes and a sample.
2. Missing values, duplicates and obviously wrong values per column.
3. Distributions for key numeric columns and top values for categoricals.
4. Three relationships most relevant to my goal, with a chart each.
5. Data-quality issues to fix before deeper analysis.

Give runnable code cells and tell me what to look for in each output.

title: KPI dashboard spec
summary: Define metrics precisely before anyone builds a chart.
body:
Write a dashboard spec for {{team}} who need to answer: {{decisions}}.

For each metric (aim for 5–8):
- Name and one-sentence definition.
- Exact formula and data source.
- Grain (daily/weekly), filters and segments.
- Target or healthy range.
- Chart type and why.

Also include: metrics we deliberately left out and why, and a note on how often data refreshes.

title: Spreadsheet formula helper
summary: Get the exact Excel / Google Sheets formula with an explanation.
body:
I'm using {{spreadsheet_app}}. My data: {{data_layout}}

I want to: {{goal}}

Give me:
1. The formula, ready to paste, with cell references matching my layout.
2. A plain explanation of each part.
3. A version that handles blanks and errors gracefully.
4. If there's a simpler approach (pivot table, filter view, QUERY), mention it.

title: Sanity-check an A/B test result
summary: Decide whether an experiment result is real before you ship it.
body:
A/B test results:
- Control: {{control_visitors}} visitors, {{control_conversions}} conversions
- Variant: {{variant_visitors}} visitors, {{variant_conversions}} conversions
- Ran for {{duration}}

1. Compute conversion rates, absolute and relative lift, and a 95% confidence interval for the difference.
2. Is it statistically significant? Was the sample large enough for the effect size?
3. Check for common traps: peeking, novelty effect, uneven traffic split, weekday effects.
4. Recommendation: ship, keep running (how long), or stop — with reasoning a non-statistician understands.

title: Landing page copy that converts
summary: Headline, sections and CTA written for one specific audience.

title: SEO blog post brief
summary: Everything a writer needs to rank for one keyword.
body:
Create an SEO content brief for the keyword "{{keyword}}" for {{site}}.

Include:
- Search intent and who is searching.
- Suggested title (under 60 chars) and meta description (under 155 chars).
- Outline with H2/H3s that fully answer the intent.
- Questions to answer (People Also Ask style).
- Internal links to add and external sources worth citing.
- What would make this better than the current top results.
- Target length and a clear CTA.

title: Product launch plan
summary: Two weeks of launch tasks across channels, day by day.
body:
Plan the launch of {{product_or_feature}} on {{launch_date}}.

Audience: {{audience}}
Channels we have: {{channels}}

Give me a day-by-day plan from T-14 to T+7 with:
- Tasks per channel (email, social, community, PR, in-app).
- The key message and one asset needed per task.
- Owner placeholder and how to measure each.
- A launch-day checklist and a "what if it flops" plan.

title: Cold email that gets replies
summary: Short, specific outreach with follow-ups.
body:
Write a cold email to {{recipient_role}} at {{company_type}} about {{offer}}.

Rules:
- Under 120 words. One idea. One ask.
- First line is about them, not us.
- Specific proof (number or named customer) if available: {{proof}}.
- Low-friction CTA (a question, not "book a 30-minute call").

Also write two follow-ups (day 3 and day 8), each shorter than the last and adding something new. Give 3 subject lines under 6 words.

title: Repurpose one piece into a week of posts
summary: Turn an article, video or talk into social content for each platform.
body:
Repurpose this content into a week of social posts:

{{source_content}}

Create:
- 3 LinkedIn posts (hook line, short paragraphs, one takeaway each).
- 5 X/Twitter posts, including one thread of 5–7 posts.
- 2 short-video scripts (under 45 seconds) with on-screen text.
- 1 newsletter blurb.

Keep the voice {{voice}}. No hashtags spam — max 2 where useful.

title: Edit for clarity without changing my voice
summary: Tighter sentences, same personality.
body:
Edit the text below for clarity and flow. Keep my voice, opinions and vocabulary.

{{text}}

Rules:
- Cut filler and repetition; shorten long sentences.
- Fix grammar and typos.
- Don't add new ideas or corporate phrasing.
- Keep it roughly the same length or shorter.

Return the edited text, then a bullet list of the 5 most important changes and why.

title: README that people actually read
summary: A clear README for any project in the right order.
body:
Write a README for {{project_name}}: {{project_description}}.

Order:
1. One-line description and who it's for.
2. Screenshot or demo placeholder.
3. Quick start (copy-paste commands, under 5 steps).
4. Configuration (table: name, required, default, description).
5. Common tasks / usage examples.
6. How it works (short, optional diagram).
7. Contributing and license.

Use short sections and code blocks. Assume the reader has 2 minutes.

title: Explain a technical topic to non-technical readers

title: Claude Code hooks: format on save and block dangerous commands
summary: A .claude/settings.json with hooks that auto-format edited files and stop risky shell commands.
body:
Add this to `.claude/settings.json` in your project (merge it with any settings you already have):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "f=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty'); [ -n \"$f\" ] && {{formatter_command}} \"$f\" || true" }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/block-dangerous.sh" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

And create `.claude/hooks/block-dangerous.sh`, then run `chmod +x .claude/hooks/block-dangerous.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Stops risky shell commands before Claude Code runs them. Needs jq.
cmd=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')
block() { echo "Blocked by project hook ($1): $cmd" >&2; exit 2; }   # exit 2 = block and tell Claude why

# Recursive delete of the root, your home folder, or the whole current folder (any flag order).
if echo "$cmd" | grep -Eq '(^|[;&|[:space:]])rm[[:space:]]([^;&|]*[[:space:]])?(-[a-zA-Z]*[rR][a-zA-Z]*|--recursive)([[:space:]]|$)' &&
   echo "$cmd" | grep -Eq '(^|[;&|[:space:]])rm[[:space:]][^;&|]*[[:space:]](/|/\*|~|~/|\$HOME|\$HOME/|\.|\./|\.\.|\*)([[:space:];&|]|$)'; then
  block "recursive delete of /, ~ or ."
fi

# Force pushes: -f, --force, --force-with-lease, or a +branch refspec.
if echo "$cmd" | grep -Eq 'git[[:space:]]+push([[:space:]]|$)' &&
   echo "$cmd" | grep -Eq '[[:space:]](-[a-zA-Z]*f[a-zA-Z]*|--force|--force-with-lease(=[^[:space:]]*)?|--force-if-includes)([[:space:]]|$)|[[:space:]]\+[^[:space:]]+'; then
  block "force push"
fi

# Destructive SQL.
if echo "$cmd" | grep -Eiq 'drop[[:space:]]+(table|database|schema)|truncate[[:space:]]+(table[[:space:]]+)?[a-z_"`]'; then
  block "destructive SQL"
fi

# Your own extra rule (an extended regex). Leave it empty to skip.
EXTRA='{{extra_blocked_pattern}}'
if [ -n "$EXTRA" ] && echo "$cmd" | grep -Eq "$EXTRA"; then
  block "project rule"
fi
exit 0
```

**Needs:** `jq` (`brew install jq` or `apt install jq`) and your formatter installed in the project (for example `npm i -D prettier`), not just available through npx.

**What it blocks:** recursive deletes of `/`, `~` or the whole current folder in any flag order (`rm -rf`, `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`), force pushes (`-f`, `--force`, `--force-with-lease`, `+branch`), `DROP TABLE/DATABASE/SCHEMA` and `TRUNCATE`, plus your extra pattern. Normal cleanups like `rm -rf node_modules` or `rm -rf /tmp/cache` still run.

**Check it:** run `/hooks` to see both hooks loaded, ask Claude to edit a file and confirm it was formatted, then ask it to run `psql -c "DROP TABLE x"` and confirm it's blocked.

---
description: Supabase conventions
globs: ["supabase/**","src/**/*.ts","app/**/*.ts"]
alwaysApply: false
---

# Supabase

- Every table: `enable row level security` plus explicit policies in the same migration. Use `(select auth.uid())` in policies.
- Schema changes only through migrations in `supabase/migrations` (`supabase migration new <name>`); never edit the remote database by hand.
- The anon key is public; the service-role key is server-only and never logged or sent to the browser.

summary: Writes clear Conventional Commits messages from the staged diff, with a body that explains why.

---
name: commit-messages
description: Write a Conventional Commits message for the staged changes. Use when the user asks to commit, write a commit message, or describe staged changes.
---

# Commit messages

1. Run `git diff --staged`. If nothing is staged, say so and stop. Don't stage files yourself unless asked.
2. Pick one type: feat, fix, refactor, perf, docs, test, build, ci, chore. Add a scope when one area is touched: `fix(auth): …`.
3. Subject: imperative, under 72 characters, no full stop. Say what changes for the user or the code, not which files.
4. Body (skip for trivial changes): why the change was needed and anything surprising. Wrap at 72 characters.
5. Footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: …` when behaviour changes for callers; `Closes #123` when an issue is referenced.

If the diff mixes unrelated changes, suggest splitting it and list the groups instead of writing one message.

Never invent context you can't see in the diff.

title: Skill: systematic debugging
summary: Makes the agent reproduce, isolate and prove a bug's cause before changing code.
body:
---
name: systematic-debugging
description: Debug a failure methodically. Use when the user reports a bug, error, failing test or unexpected behaviour and the cause isn't obvious.
---

# Systematic debugging

Do not edit code until step 4.

1. **Reproduce.** Find the smallest command, test or click path that shows the bug. Record the exact error and where it appears.
2. **Locate.** Read the code on the failing path. List the 2–4 places the bug could come from.
3. **Prove.** For each candidate, add a log, assertion or failing test that confirms or rules it out. Stop when one is proven.
4. **Fix the cause**, not the symptom. Keep the change as small as possible.
5. **Verify.** Re-run the reproduction and the nearby tests. Add a regression test if there isn't one.
6. **Report:** cause (one sentence), fix, evidence it works, and anything else that might share the cause.

If you can't reproduce it, say what you tried and what information would help. Don't guess-fix.

title: Skill: Supabase RLS review
summary: Audits Supabase tables, policies and functions for data-exposure mistakes before they ship.
body:
---
name: supabase-rls-review
description: Review Supabase row-level security. Use when the user adds or changes tables, policies, views or database functions in a Supabase project, or asks for a security check.
---

# Supabase RLS review

For each table in the change (or every table in `public` when asked for a full review):

1. **RLS enabled?** `alter table … enable row level security` must be in the same migration that creates the table.
2. **Policies match intent.** Select/insert/update/delete each considered. `using` limits rows you can see; `with check` limits rows you can write. Updates usually need both.
3. **Ownership via auth.uid()**, written as `(select auth.uid())` for performance. Never trust a user_id sent by the client.
4. **No `using (true)` on private data.** Public read is fine for public content only.
5. **Views:** use `security_invoker = true` so RLS applies.
6. **Functions:** `security definer` functions must set `search_path = ''`, check the caller themselves, and have execute revoked from `anon`/`authenticated` unless intended.
7. **Service role key** only on the server, never in client bundles or logs.

Report findings as: table → problem → exact SQL fix. Run the Supabase security advisors if available.

title: Skill: Next.js App Router conventions
summary: Keeps the agent on current App Router patterns: server components, server actions, caching and metadata.
body:
---
name: nextjs-app-router
description: Follow current Next.js App Router conventions. Use when creating or editing routes, layouts, data fetching, caching or metadata in a Next.js app with an app/ directory.
---

# Next.js App Router

- Components are **server components by default**. Add "use client" only for state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs, and keep client components small and low in the tree.
- Fetch data in server components or route handlers, not in `useEffect`.
- `params` and `searchParams` are **Promises** in recent versions: `const { slug } = await params`. Check the installed version's docs in node_modules/next/dist/docs when unsure.
- Mutations: server actions or route handlers; validate input (e.g. zod) and check auth first.
- Caching is explicit: decide per route whether it's static, revalidated or dynamic, and invalidate with tags after writes.
- Metadata via `export const metadata` or `generateMetadata`; one canonical URL per page.
- Images with next/image, fonts with next/font, links with next/link.
- Never import server-only modules (DB clients, secrets) into client components.

Before finishing: run lint, type check and build, and load the page to check the console.

---
name: incident-postmortem
description: Write a blameless incident postmortem. Use when the user shares notes, logs or a timeline from an outage or incident and wants a write-up.

# Incident postmortem

Sections:
1. **Summary:** what happened, impact (who, how many, how long), current status. Three sentences.
2. **Timeline** (UTC): detection, key decisions, mitigation, resolution.
3. **Root cause:** the technical cause and the conditions that let it happen. Ask "why" until you reach something fixable in process or design.
4. **What went well / what didn't:** detection, response, communication.
5. **Action items:** each with owner, due date and type (prevent / detect / mitigate). Specific and checkable.

title: Skill: accessibility check
summary: Reviews a page or component against the most common WCAG failures and fixes them.
body:
---
name: accessibility-check
description: Check and fix accessibility issues in UI code. Use when building or reviewing pages, forms or components, or when the user asks about a11y or WCAG.
---

# Accessibility check

Go through the component and fix what fails:

- **Semantics:** real buttons and links (not clickable divs), one h1, headings in order, lists as lists, landmarks (header, nav, main).
- **Names:** every input has a label; icon-only buttons have aria-label; images have alt (empty alt for decorative).
- **Keyboard:** everything works with Tab/Shift+Tab/Enter/Space/Escape; focus is visible; dialogs trap and return focus.
- **Contrast:** text at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text and UI parts) in both light and dark themes.
- **Motion:** respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- **Forms:** errors are announced (aria-live or aria-describedby) and say how to fix them.
- **Targets:** at least 24×24 px.

Report each issue with the fix you made. If a tool like axe or Lighthouse is available, run it and include the result.

title: Skill: safe dependency upgrades
summary: Upgrades packages one at a time with changelog checks and tests between each step.
body:
---
name: dependency-upgrade
description: Upgrade project dependencies safely. Use when the user asks to update packages, fix outdated or vulnerable dependencies, or bump a framework version.
---

# Safe dependency upgrades

1. List what's outdated (npm outdated, pip list --outdated, etc.) and what's vulnerable (npm audit, pip-audit). Show the list before changing anything.
2. Patch and minor versions can go together. Do **major versions one package at a time**.
3. For each major upgrade, read the changelog or migration guide first and list the breaking changes that affect this code (search for the APIs mentioned).
4. Upgrade, apply the needed code changes, then run lint, types, tests and a build.
5. Commit each major upgrade separately so it can be reverted alone.

Never edit lockfiles by hand. Never use --force or legacy-peer-deps to hide a conflict without explaining it. Stop and ask if an upgrade needs a runtime (Node/Python) change.

It uses a Firecrawl API key (cloud) or FIRECRAWL_API_URL for a self-hosted instance. Respect site terms and robots rules when crawling. Great for building datasets, competitive research and feeding docs into context.

**Try asking:**

body:

Authenticate with OAuth or an Apify API token as a bearer header. Actor runs consume credits on your Apify account, so watch costs, and follow each site's terms. Great for lead lists, market research and monitoring.

title: Browserbase MCP server (official, remote)

body:
Browserbase's hosted server gives an agent a cloud browser session with Stagehand-powered tools to start and end sessions, navigate, perform actions described in plain language, observe interactive elements and extract data. It needs a Browserbase API key, which the hosted endpoint takes as the browserbaseApiKey query parameter (treat the full URL as a secret). Sessions run on Browserbase's infrastructure, not your machine. Good for automating sites with no API and for scraping behind logins you own.

title: PayPal MCP server (official, remote)
summary: Create invoices, orders, products and subscriptions and look up transactions and disputes in PayPal.
body:
PayPal's hosted server lets an agent create and send invoices, create orders and payment links, manage catalog products and subscription plans, track shipments, and list transactions and disputes. You sign in with PayPal through OAuth; a sandbox endpoint (mcp.sandbox.paypal.com) exists for testing, and you should start there. Most tools need a PayPal Business account. Good for small-business billing tasks and reporting.

**Try asking:**
- "Create and send an invoice to client@example.com for 10 hours of consulting at $120/hour."
- "List transactions from the last 7 days over $500."
- "Show any open disputes and their deadlines."

**Sign-in:** OAuth in your AI tool the first time you use it.

title: Git MCP server (reference)
summary: Read and operate on local Git repositories: status, diffs, logs, branches, commits.
body:
The reference Git server from the MCP project lets an agent run git status, diff (staged and unstaged), log, show, branch, checkout, add, commit and reset on a local repository. It works only on paths you pass with --repository, and has no network push tool. Commit and reset change your working tree, so review before approving. Good for clients that lack built-in Git tools.

**Try asking:**
- "Show me the diff of my staged changes and suggest a commit message."
- "What changed in the last five commits?"
- "Create a branch called fix/login-timeout."

**Sign-in:** none needed.

title: Time MCP server (reference)
summary: Get the current time in any timezone and convert times between timezones.
body:
The reference Time server gives an agent two simple tools: get the current time for an IANA timezone and convert a time from one timezone to another. It needs no credentials and reads nothing from your system beyond the clock. Small but useful for scheduling across regions and avoiding date mistakes.

**Try asking:**
- "What time is it in Tokyo right now?"
- "If the meeting is 9am in New York, what time is it in Berlin and Sydney?"
- "How many hours until midnight UTC?"

**Sign-in:** none needed.

title: Sequential Thinking MCP server (reference)
summary: A structured scratchpad tool that helps an agent break problems into revisable, branching steps.
body:
The reference Sequential Thinking server provides a single tool the model uses to write out numbered thoughts, revise earlier ones and branch into alternatives while solving a problem. It has no external access and needs no credentials. It helps most with planning, debugging and design questions where step-by-step reasoning matters.

**Try asking:**
- "Use sequential thinking to plan the migration from REST to GraphQL for our API."
- "Think step by step about why this race condition happens."
- "Break down the launch checklist and revise it as you go."

**Sign-in:** none needed.

title: Everything MCP server (reference test server)
summary: Test server exercising every MCP feature: tools, resources, prompts, sampling, logging and more.
body:
The reference Everything server is meant for client developers: it implements sample tools, resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation, logging, progress notifications and other protocol features so you can check that an MCP client handles them. It has no real-world integrations and needs no credentials. Use it when building or debugging an MCP client, not for day-to-day work.
